slides.headline: Flamingos aren't born pink.
slides.sub: They hatch grey. The pink comes years later, from what they eat

slides.headline: Grey and fluffy at hatching
slides.body: Chicks hatch in white-grey down with straight bills. It takes several years and several moults to turn pink and grow the hooked bill.

slides.headline: The pink isn't in their genes
slides.body: Algae make carotenoid pigments, brine shrimp eat the algae, and flamingos eat both. Their bodies break the pigments down and deposit them in feathers and skin.

slides.headline: It eats with its head upside down
slides.body: Bill in the water pointing back at its feet, it sweeps side to side. Comb-like plates on the bill trap food as water rushes out.

slides.label: flamingo species, from deep orange-red to almost white
slides.body: Habitat and food vary by place and season, so the colour does too. Same pigment trick, different menus.

slides.headline: Both parents make 'milk'
slides.body: Crop milk forms in the throat and is brought up through the mouth: rich in protein and fat, fed until the chick can eat on its own.

slides.headline: You are what you eat. Literally.
slides.body: Fully sourced animal myths, debunked every week.
sources: Smithsonian's National Zoo: Why Are Flamingos Pink? And Other Flamingo Facts (2021)

caption:
American flamingo (Phoenicopterus ruber) chicks hatch grey. The famous pink arrives years later, straight from their food.

Carotenoid pigments made by algae pass up through brine shrimp into the birds, so the shade depends on what each flock eats. One more surprise: what looks like a backward-bending knee is actually the ankle. The real knee is hidden up under the feathers.

Swipe for the full story. Sources on the last slide.

Source: Smithsonian's National Zoo; Britannica.

Save this for the next time someone says flamingos are pink from birth.
